topics.title: 4th S-400 Air Defence System
bullets: India received the fourth squadron of the Russian-origin S-400 Triumf air defence missile system, completing a critical phase of the 2018 contract.
The fourth unit is slated for strategic deployment in the Rajasthan sector to significantly reinforce long-range missile and drone defence along India’s western border with Pakistan.
The fifth and final squadron under the original contract is expected by November 2026 and will likely be positioned along India’s northern border with China. Background –
India signed a government-to-government deal with Russia in October 2018 for the procurement of five S-400 Triumf squadrons at a total cost of $5.43 billion (approximately ₹40,000 crore).
The deal included the supply of the missile systems, associated radar systems, support equipment, and training for IAF personnel.
Under the original delivery schedule, the first squadron was to be delivered by April 2023, with all five squadrons to be completed within 45–60 months of the contract signing but were delayed.
The system can transition from traveling mode to full combat readiness in just five minutes, this is five times faster than the US Patriot system, which takes about 25 minutes to deploy.
The deployment will complete India’s initial S-400 coverage, covering all major threat axes – Pakistan (west), China (north), and the Indian Ocean Region.

Russia has been India’s largest defense partner for decades, supplying major platforms including MiG fighter jets, T-90 tanks, Sukhoi Su-30MKI aircraft, and Kilo-class submarines. India’s Defense Systems –
Project Kusha is India’s indigenous extended-range air defence system, developed by the DRDO, designed to intercept ballistic missiles and aircraft at ranges of 150–350 km.
It is intended to serve as the “Indian Iron Dome” , filling the gap between the S-400 (400 km) and medium-range systems like Barak-8 (70–150 km).
The system is expected to be inducted by 2028-29, with trials ongoing. It will feature advanced multi-function radars and a network-centric architecture.
The Akash (Sky) is a mid-range surface-to-air missile system, developed by DRDO under the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP) . Development began in 1983.
The Akash missile was inducted into the Indian Air Force in July 2015 and into the Indian Army in May 2015. It has a range of 30– 35 km and can reach speeds of Mach 2.8 to 3.5.
Akash is a mobile system capable of engaging multiple targets simultaneously, including fighter jets, drones, and cruise missiles. It has been successfully deployed in combat areas.
Akash-NG (New Generation) is an upgraded variant with improved range, accuracy, and mobility, designed to replace older systems in the IAF’s inventory.
It features a lighter, more compact launcher and advanced seeker technology, with a range of approximately 50–60 km.
Successful flight tests of Akash-NG were conducted in January 2024, and the system is expected to be inducted soon to replace legacy air defence systems.
Barak-8 is a medium-range surface-to-air missile (MRSAM) system jointly developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and DRDO, with the backing of Israeli and Indian defence firms.

The IAF variant was inducted in September 2021, and the naval version (LRSAM) is already deployed on Indian warships. The deal for the IAF version was valued at approximately $1.6 billion, signed in 2017.
Barak-8 has a range of 70 km (extended-range version up to 150 km) and a maximum speed of Mach 2. It can engage multiple aerial threats simultaneously, including aircraft, missiles, and drones.
During Operation Sindoor (May 2025), the Barak-8 system successfully intercepted a Pakistani ballistic missile (presumably Shaheen-II or Fatah variant) intended for New Delhi.
The intercept took place over the skies of Sirsa, Haryana, showcasing the system’s reliability and lethality in a real combat scenario.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh called Barak-8 a “game changer” , stating it is capable of hitting multiple targets simultaneously even in bad weather.
India’s Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) Programme was launched in 1999 following the Kargil War, in response to missile threats from Pakistan and China.
Two-tiered “multi-layered” shield: High-altitude exo-atmospheric interceptors and low-altitude endo-atmospheric interceptors.
With the successful test of the Prithvi Air Defence in November 2006, India became the fourth country (after the US, Russia, and Israel) to develop an anti-ballistic missile system.
Part of India’s two-tier Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) programme, begun in 1999 after the Kargil War. The first test was in November 2006.
Designed to intercept incoming ballistic missiles outside the Earth’s atmosphere (exo-atmospheric) at altitudes of 50-80 km.
Forms the high-altitude layer of India’s missile shield. The Prithvi Air Defence was later succeeded by the Prithvi Defence Vehicle (PDV) and the Pradyumna interceptor family.
First successful test conducted on 27 November 2006, when it destroyed an incoming “enemy” Prithvi ballistic missile at 50 km altitude.
Uses a dual-stage rocket motor based on the Prithvi missile’s propulsion system to reach altitudes of up to 80 km.
Capable of engaging targets moving at speeds of up to Mach 5, using an advanced “hit-to-kill” (kinetic) warhead.
Short-range, quick-reaction system (QRSAM) is for the Indian Army to protect moving armoured columns from aerial attacks. Its development trials were completed by 2019.
The canister-based missile has a range of 25-30 km and a speed of up to Mach 4.7, and can engage aircraft, drones, and missiles.
Mounted on a truck-based launch platform for high mobility. Induction into the Army began in 2024.

India is developing a multi-layered integrated air and missile defence system, informally called “Sudarshan Chakra” (India’s own Iron Dome), comprising: ➢Long-range (400 km): S-400 Triumf ➢Extended-range (150–350 km): Project Kusha (indigenous) ➢Medium-range (70–150 km): Barak-8 (MRSAM) ➢Short-range (30–35 km): Akash and Akash-NG
The system will be linked through a common automated command and control network (IACCS) , ensuring seamless integration of Russian, Israeli, and indigenous systems.
This layered architecture ensures that even if a threat bypasses one layer, it will be met by a wall of secondary and tertiary fire. Recent News –
The Indian Air Force completed the pre-dispatch inspection of the fourth S-400 system in Russia on 18 April 2026, ensuring the system met all technical and operational specifications.
The system was shipped using a multimodal strategy: bulky components by sea, and time-sensitive parts (radars, missiles) by heavy-lift aircraft (Il-76, C-17).
The system is expected to arrive in India by mid-May 2026, a few days after the first anniversary of Operation Sindoor (7 May 2025).

The fourth S-400 unit is specifically earmarked for deployment in the Rajasthan and Punjab sectors, areas that historically faced challenges in intercepting fast-moving aerial attacks due to flat, semi- desert terrain.

The 91N6E panoramic radar of the S-400 provides a seamless, gap- free shield, capable of monitoring high-threat zones – including terror launch pads in Bahawalpur and Muridke – from deep within Indian territory.
By the time a threat is launched from 150 km inside the border, the S-400 has already locked on, providing a decisive early-warning advantage integrated with India’s existing air defence network.
India has decided to purchase 280 short and long-range S-400 missiles to replenish stockpiles used during Operation Sindoor and to create a reserve of long-range weapons.
This replenishment package includes 120 short-range missiles and 168 long-range missiles, with an estimated cost of about $1.2 billion.
India is estimated to have fired 11 long-range S-400 missiles at Pakistan during Operation Sindoor, hitting fighter jets, early warning systems, and transport aircraft.
In March 2026, the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, granted Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) for the procurement of five more S-400 systems from Russia.
This additional procurement would raise India’s total S-400 inventory from five to ten squadrons over time, significantly expanding the country’s air defence coverage.
The S-400 systems were reportedly used by the IAF during Operation Sindoor (May 2025).

The three existing S-400 squadrons (localised under the name ‘Sudarshan Chakra’ ) established a credible defence grid against Pakistani aerial threats, including fighter jets, early warning systems, and transport aircraft.
The S-400 deal is one of India’s largest defence procurements, reflecting the government’s priority on modernising military capabilities amidst evolving regional threats.

The DAC is the highest decision-making body in the Ministry of Defence for capital procurement, headed by the Defence Minister, with the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) and three service chiefs as members.
The DAC’s approval is required for all major defence acquisitions, including the S-400 deal, Rafale jets, and indigenous systems like Project Kusha.
The DAC’s Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) is the first step in the procurement process, followed by technical evaluation, cost negotiation, and contract finalisation.

The S-400 system is integrated into the IAF’s Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) , a network that combines inputs from military and civilian radars, airborne early warning aircraft, and ground sensors.
This integration enables real-time data sharing between the S- 400, Barak-8, Akash, and other air defence systems, creating a unified, networked defence grid.
The IACCS is a prime example of jointness and interoperability – a key focus of India’s military reforms, including the creation of theatre commands under the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) .

topics.title: Press Freedom Rights
bullets: During PM Modi’s visit to the Netherlands on 16 May 2026, a briefing turned contentious after Dutch journalists questioned an Indian diplomat over concerns about press freedom and minority rights in India.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten expressed concern ahead of his meeting with PM Modi about the erosion of press freedom, triggering a sharp response from Delhi.
The World Press Freedom Index 2026 ranks India at 157 out of 180 countries, a decline of six places from the previous year, placing it in the “very serious” category. What is Press Freedom? –
Press freedom is the right of the media to publish news, opinions, and information without government interference or censorship.
It is considered a cornerstone of democracy, enabling public debate, holding governments accountable, and serving as a “watchdog” on power.
In India, press freedom is not an independent right but is derived from the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
Article 19(1)(a) guarantees to all citizens the right to freedom of speech and expression.
In 1950, the Supreme Court in Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras, 1950, observed that freedom of the press lay at the foundation of all democratic organisations.
The landmark case of Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1958) established that press freedom includes the right of free publication and circulation, free from interference from authority.
The right under Article 19(1)(a) is not absolute. Article 19(2) empowers the State to impose “reasonable restrictions” on this freedom.
Restrictions can be imposed in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation, or incitement to an offence.
The key phrase is “reasonable restrictions,” meaning any restriction must be proportionate, non-arbitrary, and have a rational nexus with the stated objective.
The Press Council of India is a statutory, quasi-judicial body established under the Press Council Act, 1978, replacing a non- statutory council set up in 1966.
Its primary objective is to preserve press freedom and improve newspaper and news agency standards.
The PCI has civil court powers (summoning witnesses, demanding documents), but its punitive powers are limited to censure; it also builds a code of conduct and fosters public responsibility.
The News Broadcasters and Digital Association (NBDA) is the apex body of news broadcasters, digital news publishers, and media networks in India established in 2007.
It plays a key role in self-regulation by formulating ethical guidelines and a Code of Conduct for its members.
The NBDA also addresses grievances through its self-regulatory body, the News Broadcasting & Digital Standards Authority (NBDSA).
First Press Commission (1952-54) recommended establishing the Press Council of India to regulate and maintain press standards.
Second Press Commission (1982) made 278 recommendations, including empowering the Press Council, protecting press freedom via Industries Act amendment, and codifying parliamentary privileges.
Chanda Committee (1964-66) recommended separating AIR and Doordarshan as autonomous corporations; this was implemented on 1 April 1976. What is Press Freedom Index ? –
The report has been published every year since 2002 by Reporters Without Borders or Reporters Sans Frontieres (RSF).
It develops a score between 0 (for the worst possible performance in terms of securing press freedom) and 100 (the best possible score).
A score below 70 falls under the ‘problematic’ category. Source: Indian Express

This score is based on two indicators: 1) A tally of abuses against media and journalists in connection with their work. 2) A qualitative analysis of the situation in each country or territory based on the responses of “press freedom specialists”, including journalists, researchers, academics and human rights defenders, to an RSF questionnaire of 100 questions available in 24 languages.

In the questionnaire for qualitative analysis, having more than 100 questions, each country’s score is evaluated after assessment of the state of media across five factors: 1. the political context 2. legal framework 3. economic context 4. sociocultural context 5. safety.
Reporters Without Borders or Reporters Sans Frontiers (in French) is a global media watchdog headquartered in Paris, France.
It was founded in 1985 and recognised as a public interest organisation in France since 1995.
RSF has consultative status with the United Nations, UNESCO, the Council of Europe and the International Organization of Francophonie (OIF). 2026 Report Highlights –
India has slipped to the 157th position out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, a drop of six places from its 2025 rank of 151st.
This continues a downward trend, placing India within the “very serious” category of the index and solidifying its status as one of the world’s most challenging environments for independent media.
For the first time, India now trails behind its neighbours Pakistan (153rd) and Bangladesh (152nd) in the rankings.
Norway continues to top the index for the tenth consecutive year, with a score of 92.72.
It is followed by the Netherlands (88.92) , Estonia (88.54) , Denmark (88.47) , and Sweden (87.61) .
The top ten are all European nations, reflecting a longstanding trend of high press freedom in the region.
The lowest-ranked countries are Eritrea (180th) , North Korea (179th) , China (178th) , Iran (177th) , and Syria (176th) .
Eritrea has remained at the bottom for the third consecutive year, while Iran dropped one place to 177th.
China remains among the most restrictive environments globally, with journalism effectively criminalised.
The United States dropped seven places to 64th (from 57th in 2025), citing political polarisation and legal threats.
Russia ranks 172nd in the “very serious” category, where independent journalism is effectively criminalised.
Ukraine rose seven places to 55th , gaining 50 positions since the full-scale invasion began.
Palestine (156th) , despite the catastrophic war conditions, ranks just one spot above India.
For the first time since the index began in 2002, more than half of all countries (52.2%) now fall into the "difficult" or "very serious" categories for press freedom, compared to just 13.7% in 2002.
The average global score across all 180 countries has never been so low in the index's 25-year history, indicating a sustained global deterioration in media independence.

The share of the world's population living in a country where press freedom is considered "good" has plummeted from 20% to less than 1%; only seven northern European countries now qualify. South Asia Highlights –
India now ranks below Nepal (87th), Maldives (108th), Sri Lanka (134th), Bhutan (150th), Bangladesh (152nd), and Pakistan (153rd) — a significant reversal from previous years.
Nepal is the highest-ranked in South Asia at 87th, but the report notes that its strong global ranking masks rising attacks, legal pressure, and economic fragility in the media sector.
Afghanistan ranks 175th, with 43% of media outlets shut down since the Taliban returned to power and 80% of women journalists no longer active.

At least 15 journalists have been charged under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA) as of 2024, with watchdogs calling out the government for "targeting and prosecuting journalists" using anti-terror laws.
The report heavily criticised the concentration of media ownership by conglomerates closely aligned with the ruling government, citing acquisitions of NDTV and The Quint as examples.
RSF pointed to the use of "lawfare tactics" (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation — SLAPPs) to intimidate and harass journalists, deterring media investigation into large businesses
Of the five indicators (political, legal, economic, sociocultural, safety), the legal indicator deteriorated the most, worsening in 110 out of 180 countries.
Syria recorded the largest global jump, advancing 36 places to 141st, following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 and the country's transition to a new political phase.
Niger suffered the world's biggest drop, falling 37 places due to armed attacks and military repression. World Press Freedom Day –
Observed annually on May 3rd.
It was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in 1993 after UNESCO’s recommendation in 1991 Windhoek Declaration.

The day picked for the purpose was May 3— the anniversary of the Declaration of Windhoek on Promoting an Independent and Pluralistic African Press, made in 1992 at a UNESCO seminar held in Windhoek, Namibia.
The global theme for 2026 was "Shaping a Future at Peace" – focusing on how press freedom contributes to peace, conflict prevention and resilient information societies.
UNESCO hosted the 33rd World Press Freedom Day Conference in Lusaka, Zambia on 4 May 2026 in a hybrid format.
The conference brings together journalists, policymakers, academics and civil society to reaffirm freedom of expression as a pillar for the future of information societies.
